title: Gene structure and frequencies across populations

segs.text: Section seven. Gene structure and frequencies across populations. Two figures from Goodman and Gilman's close the day. The first reviews the parts of a gene where variants can occur. The promoter is where the machinery for expressing the gene starts. Exons are the D N A that ends up as amino acid sequence. Introns were once thought meaningless, but variations are now known to occur there. A stop codon sits at the end. Variants are sorted into those changing protein abundance, those changing the protein product, and markers for nearby or distant functional variation.

The second figure shows that how often each allele or phenotype occurs differs widely between populations. The point is that frequencies vary. For C Y P three A five, star one is the wild type, and star three, star six and star seven are non-functional. In sub-Saharan African populations, star one is common and all three variants are present. In European populations there are relatively few wild type alleles, and most are star three.

For V K O R C one minus sixteen thirty nine, G to A, the G allele means a higher dose is required and the A allele a lower dose, and the two are compared across African, European and North American, and East Asian populations. For T P M T, most people are normal metabolizers, with only a small bar of poor metabolizers. N U D T fifteen comes later; its sub-Saharan African data are currently unknown.

Frequency together with the severity of the toxicity decides how much to worry about a variant, including whether to genotype everyone from a population. Azathioprine and six mercaptopurine are metabolized by T P M T. Only a few people may be T P M T poor metabolizers, but a poor metabolizer given the normal dose could die. She said, Those people need less than ten percent of the normal dose. So a rare phenotype can still justify genotyping, because the toxicity is severe.
